title: My hometown voted Republican for 50 years. Then came an election shaped by economic frustration | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

If you find yourself in Colorado Springs, Colorado, do yourself a favor and head to the Mesa Overlook, where the red sandstone formations of the Garden of the Gods tower above the high-desert grasslands while the magnificent Pikes Peak stands watch.

It’s a one-of-a-kind view in a city that has no shortage of distinctive experiences.

As someone who grew up there, I could go on and on about the landscape, the history, and just how good Red Top’s massive hamburgers were.

As a former resident who visits frequently, I could share how much the city has changed and grown.

And as a reporter covering the economy, I can relay how some residents of my hometown – like those in many other cities across the country – are enduring the financial gut punches that come with an energy price shock and five-plus years of high inflation.

Those changes – in the city itself and in the increasing affordability concerns its residents face – help tell the story of why, for the first time in more than 50 years, my hometown elected a Democrat to Congress.

Colorado Springs has long been a conservative bastion. It’s a city with military installations to its north, east, south and southwest. It’s an evangelical hub, serving as the headquarters to ministries like Young Life and Focus on the Family.

And while the 2026 midterm elections brought a slew of unexpected outcomes across the nation, the Colorado District 5 race still took me aback: Democrat Jessica Killin, who won 50.5% of the vote, unseated Republican Jeff Crank (who received 45.8%).

Republicans have easily carried this district since it was formed in 1972. So, what changed this cycle?

First, the Springs has been on a massive growth spurt since well before I was born.

With its majestic purple mountains; its beautiful, spacious skies; and its wealth of other amenities, Colorado Springs has long attracted newcomers.

In 1970, about 135,000 people lived there. It’s since tripled in size to a half-million peopleand could soon overtake Denver as Colorado’s largest city. (Denver, which is a consolidated city and county is more geographically limited.)

But now, as Colorado Springs’ urban core is getting bigger and busier, the population mix is changing, said Steven Pittz, a political science professor at the University of Colorado Colorado Springs (UCCS).

“In the past 10 to 15 years, we’ve had more young people moving (to the Springs) to be closer to that mountain lifestyle and a place that’s a little bit cheaper than Boulder, Denver, etc.,” he said.

The influx that Pittz referenced has been apparent on my visits home during that time.

Of course, it feels like I’ve seen more out-of-state license plates or heard more mispronunciations of streets like Nevada, Tejon and Uintah; but many of my conversations and interactions have been with folks who moved to the Springs in the past 15 years.

In the past couple of decades, I’ve witnessed open prairies be slowly overtaken by sprawling, cul-de-sac-laden subdivisions; the humble scrub oak on the face of Cheyenne Mountain be supplanted by million-dollar homes; and a lonely road on the east side of the Springs turn into a six-lane artery that now sits as the center of town.

It’s the type of growth that you can just feel. But to be honest, it hasn’t seemed too out of place for Colorado Springs.

The region has long served as a magnet: Thousands of years ago, it was a “cultural crossroads” for many indigenous tribes; in 1871, Colorado Springs was founded as a resort town, and, soon thereafter, became a health and wellness destination for tuberculosis patients; and by World War I, it started establishing itself as a military hub.

The region has also changed through the realignment of Colorado’s congressional districts: District 5 went from including several conservative, rural counties to primarily El Paso County. It wentfrom being a heavily Republican district to one where unaffiliated voters have the slight majority, followed by Republicans and then Democrats, Pittz said.

He sees Colorado Springs and the Centennial State of Colorado being reflections of the “great sorting,” where people coalesce with others who align politically. Red states are becoming redder, blue states bluer, he said.

“When I think about Colorado, and then I think about Colorado Springs,” he said, “there’s this question of, ‘How long do you remain a Republican stronghold in a state that continues to sort in that direction?’”

Pittz said he wouldn’t be surprised if a Republican retakes District 5 in the next election cycle or two. However, he added, the 2026 race showed that it’s possible Colorado Springs could become a politically purple city (or at least a maroon one).

For example, in 2024, President Donald Trump won the district by a relatively small margin; and in 2022, outgoing Democratic Governor Jared Polis carried the city, said John Suthers, a former Colorado attorney general and Republican who served as Colorado Springs’ mayor from 2015 to 2023.

“For those of us who paid close attention, we realized that the demographics of the district had changed,” Suthers said. “Having said that, I will tell you, Jessica Killin won because it was a referendum on (President) Donald Trump.”

At the heart of that referendum, Suthers said, were the negative consequences from two of Trump’s major decisions: tariffs and a war with Iran.

“I’m not the most economically sophisticated person in the world, but I’m economically sophisticated enough to know that tariffs drive up prices,” Suthers said, adding they also run counterintuitive to Republicans who embraced free enterprise and free trade. “Small businesses are impacted by that, and everybody felt that.”

“Then, all of a sudden, next thing you know, we’re in a war with Iran … and all of a sudden, we’re paying $4.60 for a gallon of gas,” he added.

The negative economic sentiment caused a shift in the political winds among many in the Springs. And that included Suthers’ own Republican-heavy neighborhood nestled at the foothills of the Rocky Mountains where Killin’s yard signs outnumbered Crank’s by three to one, he said.

“The Democrats were highly, highly motivated,” Suthers said. “But I know there were Republican neighbors of mine who said, ‘I’m through, and we’re voting Democrat.’ And if you talk to them, it was all economics.”

When you grow up in a single-parent family that’s hugging the poverty line, it’s easy to recognize some actions undertaken by those struggling to make ends meet.

There’s a financial triage that occurs.

First goes the discretionary spending. That includes nixing the already modest summer trip up I-25 to Denver to see the zoo, or the museum, or the fantastically unique Casa Bonita. Also, dining out becomes a luxury, and Olive Garden and Outback become special-occasion-only locales.

And it doesn’t take too long for the belt-tightening to show up at the gas station – a $10 check would be cut to put enough in the tank to make it to payday; or at the grocery store – where shopping lists shrank and mental math took place the register; or to the discount retailer – where sales were scoured to get one new item to add to last year’s wardrobe.

The hope is that the cuts made along the way prevent a deeper wounding. But sometimes, not even the electric bill, the insurance statement or the mortgage were safe.

This type of pain and these types of actions aren’t always visible to outsiders.

However, with each trip back home, I’ve noticed more potential signs that residents are experiencing increased financial strain: At the supermarket checkout, I witnessed a customer put back a box of cereal and a tube of ground beef, relegating the items from ‘nice to have’ to ‘cannot afford.’ At the gas station, the pump totals – $10 even, $20 even, $7 even — tell a story of drivers putting just enough gas in their tanks to get by.

But beyond the decisions at the grocery store and the minimal fuel fill-ups, it’s also the foot-traffic dropping off at certain stores and restaurants, the longer lines at the food banks, and the increase in folks experiencing homelessness.

Even as Colorado Springs’ population is growing and the economy is expanding, the city was short 27,700 housing units in 2023 and has a need for 60,000 more by 2035, a recent city assessment showed. Household budgets were running short as well: Roughly two-thirds of renters and homeowners arespending more than 30% of their income on housing costs.

Unsurprisingly, cost-of-living concerns were front and center on the campaign trail this election, Killin told CNN in an interview.

“Just like we’re hearing across the country, people here in El Paso County, they’re struggling,” she said in an interview days after her victory. “This is still a relatively affordable place compared to the rest of the Front Range in Colorado, but it’s growing increasingly unaffordable.”

And it wasn’t just housing, said Killin, a fourth-generation Coloradan who grew up in the Springs.

Rising healthcare costs, childcare costs, and business costs were weighing on people, she noted. And in the military-centric Springs, many veterans’ cost-of-living concerns were compounded by negative sentiment about the Iran war and its potential effects on national security and ally relationships, said Killin, an Army veteran herself.

But above all, people told her that they feel like they can’t get ahead, she said.

“They feel like the American Dream isn’t in reach anymore, and they want an economy that works for more people, not just the lucky few,” she said.
